## Executive Summary

America's STEM future is being decided before children can read — and we are losing ground. The most recent Nation's Report Card shows just 31% of U.S. 8th graders reached proficiency in science in 2024, the worst result in over a decade, with 12th-grade math hitting a record low of 22% proficient (NAGB/NCES, 2025). The root cause sits upstream: K-3 classrooms devote a mere 18 minutes a day to science, against 89 for reading and 57 for math (Horizon Research, 2019). Children are not failing science — the system is failing to introduce it during the exact developmental window when curiosity and identity take shape.

That window is unforgiving, especially for girls. By age 6, girls become less likely than boys to associate brilliance with their own gender and begin avoiding activities for the "really, really smart" — a gap absent at age 5 (Bian, Leslie & Cimpian / *Science*, 2017). The damage compounds: the share of U.S. girls who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% to 59% (ROX Girls' Index, 2024), and women remain just 26% of the STEM workforce (AAUW, 2023). Meanwhile, families are caught in a screen-time paradox — children ages 5-8 average 3.5 hours of daily screen media (Common Sense Media, 2025) — even as 78% of parents say they want more toys that build creativity and problem-solving (The Toy Association, 2025).

The market is large but fragmented. The U.S. educational toys market is projected to roughly double to about $24.6 billion by 2033 (Custom Market Insights, 2024), and U.S. EdTech will reach $90.6 billion by 2030, with preschool its fastest-growing segment (Grand View Research, 2024). Yet today's offerings are siloed: KiwiCo and Lovevery sell kits, Khan Academy Kids is an app, Osmo bolts pieces onto a tablet. None fuses serialized story, a hands-on kit, an AI companion, and diverse girl role models. That siloing drives churn — over one-third of subscribers cancel within three months (McKinsey, 2018) — because a disconnected craft-of-the-month gives kids no reason to return.

This is the white space PARI STEAM World occupies. The evidence is unusually aligned: hands-on active learning lifts performance by 0.47 standard deviations (Freeman et al. / PNAS, 2014); relatable STEM characters change real behavior, with heavy female *X-Files* viewers 50% more likely to have worked in STEM (Geena Davis Institute, 2018); and AI gains are real when it augments human guidance (Stanford Tutor CoPilot, 2024). PARI integrates all four proven levers — story, kit, supervised AI, and representation — into one engagement spine, intervening in early childhood before curiosity erodes and stereotypes harden. It is the only product purpose-built for the moment that matters most.

missingTopics: No unit economics or business-model proof for PARI itself: CAC, LTV, gross margin, COGS of a physical kit + AI, pricing tier, or a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM. The dossier sizes adjacent markets (educational toys, EdTech, tutoring) but never sizes PARI's realistic obtainable share or what a subscriber is worth. A skeptical investor's first question — 'how big is YOUR business and at what price/margin' — is unanswered.

No efficacy evidence for the PARI product or format itself. All learning-outcome evidence is borrowed proxies (Freeman is undergraduate STEM lectures; Scully is adult women recalling a 1990s TV character; Tutor CoPilot is human tutors, not a kit/app). There is zero pilot, learning-gain, or engagement data on PARI's own story+kit+AI model for ages 3–8.

AI cost, safety, and COPPA/child-data regulatory exposure. The paper leans on an 'AI companion' for under-8s but never addresses COPPA, FTC enforcement, child-data privacy, AI content-safety/hallucination risk for young children, or the cost of running AI per user — the exact concerns the dossier itself flags (25% of teachers distrust AI; parents worry about child data).

Competitive response and moat/defensibility. The 'no one integrates story+kit+AI' white space is asserted but the paper never addresses why incumbents (KiwiCo, Lovevery, well-funded) couldn't add a story layer or AI companion, nor IP/brand/content moat. Also omits direct girl-forward STEM competitors (GoldieBlox, Girls Who Code, Black Girls Code, Goldie Blox, Roominate, Wonder Workshop, Encyclopedia/Doc McStuffins, Ada Twist Scientist) — the competitive set is incomplete.

Distribution and go-to-market: retail vs DTC vs school channel, partnerships, customer-acquisition strategy in a high-CAC DTC subscription market. The dossier flags brutal subscription churn (40% cancel, 10–15% monthly) but the paper offers only 'serialized story fixes churn' as an assertion, with no retention data for the proposed format.

Reading-age / developmental-fit feasibility for ages 3–8: the target audience largely cannot read serialized text independently, implying heavy parent or audio mediation. No evidence the story-driven model works for pre-readers, nor data on parent time-burden, a known churn driver for kits.

Willingness-to-pay at PARI's specific price point and for a specific demographic. Enrichment-spend data is heavily skewed to the affluent top quintile (~$8,900 vs ~$1,300); the 'democratize access' claim has no pricing or affordability model showing how a premium integrated kit+AI reaches beyond that quintile.

Boys / universal-market sizing. The product is positioned 'girl-forward,' but the paper never quantifies whether narrowing to girls halves the TAM or whether boys are addressable, nor how a girl-forward brand performs commercially (mixed track record of girl-targeted STEM toys is unaddressed).

International benchmark for what works in early-childhood STEAM specifically (most cited efficacy evidence is K-12/undergrad or media, not ages 3–8 product interventions). No citation of early-childhood-specific intervention RCTs (e.g., Head Start STEM, Sesame/PBS Kids efficacy, Ramani & Siegler number-board studies) that would directly support the 3–8 thesis.
unsupportedClaims: 'Serialized storytelling + a persistent companion gives a structural retention advantage over single-format boxes.' This is asserted across the Competitive and Market-Gap sections, but no data in the dossier measures retention of a story-driven or AI-companion subscription. The churn stats (McKinsey, SubJolt) describe generic boxes; there is no evidence that adding story/AI lowers churn.

'AI as a supervised, parent-governed co-pilot.' The dossier's AI evidence (Tutor CoPilot) is about AI assisting trained human tutors, not a parent-supervised AI for a 3–8-year-old. The leap from 'AI helps tutors' to 'parent-governed AI companion for preschoolers raises learning' is unsupported.

'PARI democratizes access / closes the equity gap.' The enrichment-gap data show affluent families outspend the lowest quintile ~7:1, but nothing shows PARI is priced or distributed to reach lower-income families; given premium comps ($24–40/mo + AI cost), the affordability/democratization claim is unbacked.

The 'Scully Effect' is repeatedly used to argue a girl protagonist will change young children's STEM behavior, but the study surveyed women aged 25+ recalling an adult-targeted 1990s drama. It is correlational (viewers self-select) and has no bearing on whether a fictional girl character changes outcomes for ages 3–8. Using it as causal proof for the early-childhood thesis overstates it.

Freeman et al. active-learning gains (+0.47 SD) are presented as support for the hands-on/kit premise, but the study is exclusively undergraduate STEM lecture-vs-active-learning. Extending a college-classroom effect size to a home STEAM kit for preschoolers is an unsupported extrapolation (the dossier flags this as 'directional' but the section likely uses it as stronger than that).

Heckman's ~13% ROI is a return on intensive birth-to-five disadvantaged-child programs (ABC/CARE), not on a consumer STEAM toy/subscription. Citing it to imply PARI yields comparable returns conflates a wraparound social program with a retail product.

'No major incumbent centers diverse girl protagonists in an integrated story+kit+AI format.' The 'integrated story+kit+AI' part may be true, but 'diverse girl protagonists in early STEM' is a crowded space (GoldieBlox, Ada Twist/Doc McStuffins media, Goldie Blox, etc.); the claim of an empty position overstates the white space unless narrowed strictly to the tri-format combination.

Implied causation that ~18 min/day of K-3 science 'causes' the downstream interest/achievement declines. The instructional-time and the achievement/interest figures are from different studies; the dossier presents correlation, not a demonstrated causal chain, yet the narrative treats reduced science time as the cause.
weakestStats: The US educational-toys market endpoint is internally inconsistent across the dossier: ~$13.66B by 2030 (GVR Horizon, the dimension's own verified correction), ~$24.86B by 2030 (Screen-Time dimension), and ~$24.6B by 2033 (Custom Market Insights, used in Parent-Attitudes and Competitive dimensions). Three conflicting endpoints/years for the single most important sizing number. Must be reconciled to one figure or the paper loses credibility.

US STEM-toys segment size conflicts by >5x: ~$340M (GVR, ~80% of NA, 2024) in Market Size vs ~$1.8B (Global Market Insights, ~85% of NA, 2024) in Screen-Time. Pick one source/definition; the $1.8B/85%-share figure is from a weaker vendor and contradicts the GVR North-America base.

Junior Achievement '9% of teen girls interested in a STEM career' (2019, fielded April 2019, n=1,004, vendor-commissioned by 'Engine'). It is 7 years stale, a commissioned single survey, about teens (13–17) not the 3–8 target, and is used as a current headline. Replace with current data or clearly date-flag it.

Custom Market Insights US educational-toys figures ($11.1B→$24.6B, 9.2% CAGR) are from a low-tier vendor and conflict with GVR; flagged even in the dossier as 'vendor market-research estimate.' Harden by leading with GVR/Fortune Business Insights or drop.

Women's share of the US STEM workforce is cited as 35%, 27%, 26%, and 24% across dimensions (different denominators: broad STEM vs core S&E vs Census 2019 vs Geena Davis). Used semi-interchangeably; standardize on the most recent NCSES definition and state the denominator each time.

STEM job-growth figures conflict by vintage: 10.4% (2023–2033, BLS/DOL) vs 7% (2022–2032, NCSES) vs 12.5% (S&E). Lead with the newest BLS projection and drop the older 7% to avoid a same-paper contradiction.

SubJolt '10–15% monthly subscription-box churn' (2026, undated industry blog) is a weak, non-peer-reviewed benchmark used to size a core retention argument; corroborate with a primary source or present as illustrative only.

PISA 'rank' framing is inconsistent: '28th of 37 OECD' (Parent-Attitudes) vs '25 systems scored higher / 9 systems higher in science' out of 80 participants (State-of-STEM). Different denominators (OECD-37 vs all-80) make the US look alternately worse/better; standardize.

The 'Scully Effect' correlational figures (50% more likely to have worked in STEM, 24% vs 16%) are self-selection-prone and from an advocacy institute (Geena Davis / 21st Century Fox), about adults recalling 1990s TV. Weak as causal evidence for an early-childhood product; present strictly as suggestive.

Toy Association '76% want a STEM career for their child' (2019) and '78% want skill-building toys' are vendor/advocacy surveys reported second-hand (via RobotLab, Grand View Research) rather than from the primary Toy Association release; source the originals and note potential industry bias.

ABC/CARE 13% ROI (Heckman 2017) is from a tiny, decades-old, highly disadvantaged birth-to-five intervention; using it to imply returns for a consumer STEAM product is a category mismatch — weakest stat for the commercial argument even if academically sound.
suggestedAdditions: Add a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM and unit-economics box: US households with kids 3–8, share affluent enough for the price point, target price/ARPU, kit COGS + AI inference cost, gross margin, blended CAC, and projected LTV/churn. This converts adjacent-market sizing into a defensible business case.

Reconcile all market-size figures into one sourced table with explicit denominators, vintages, and a single chosen headline (recommend GVR US educational toys ~$12.19B 2023 → ~$13.66B 2030, and GVR US STEM toys ~$340M); footnote the discarded Custom Market Insights / Global Market Insights numbers.

Add a dedicated competitive table that includes direct girl-forward early-STEM players (GoldieBlox, Wonder Workshop, Encyclopedia of girl-scientist media like Ada Twist/Doc McStuffins, Roominate, Goldieblox) alongside KiwiCo/Lovevery/MEL/Osmo/Khan, with columns for story, kit, app, AI, girl-protagonist, price — so the tri-format white space is shown, not asserted.

Add a COPPA / child-data-privacy / AI-safety section: how the AI companion complies with COPPA and FTC guidance, content-moderation/hallucination guardrails for under-8s, and data handling. This directly answers the dossier's own flagged trust barrier and is table-stakes for an early-childhood AI product.

Add early-childhood-specific efficacy evidence (ages 3–8), e.g., PBS Kids / Sesame Workshop STEM efficacy studies, Ramani & Siegler numerical board-game RCTs, Head Start CREATE/early-STEM trials, to replace or supplement the undergraduate (Freeman) and adult (Scully) proxies that don't fit the target age.

Commit to a PARI pilot/efficacy plan and present any early signal: a small pre/post learning-gain or engagement/retention study on the actual story+kit+AI format. Even a pilot design with success metrics would materially de-risk the 'it works' claim that is currently entirely borrowed.

Add a retention/churn-mitigation model grounded in evidence: cite serialized-content retention from analogous categories (e.g., serialized kids' media, episodic subscription cohorts) rather than asserting story 'fixes' churn; show a target churn curve vs the 10–15% benchmark.

Add an affordability/equity mechanism if 'democratization' is retained: tiered pricing, school/Title-I channel, scholarships, or library partnerships, with a path to reach beyond the top income quintile — otherwise drop the democratization claim to avoid an unbacked promise.

Date-flag and freshen the stalest demand stats: replace 2019 Junior Achievement teen-girl interest with the most recent equivalent, and clearly label every survey with year, sample, sponsor, and whether vendor-commissioned, so the evidence base reads as current and independent.

Add a 'limitations of the evidence' paragraph acknowledging that the strongest causal studies (Freeman, Tutor CoPilot, Scully) are outside the 3–8 home-product context — pre-empting the skeptical reader by showing the team knows the proxies' limits and is testing the actual model.
critic.overallAssessment: The dossier is unusually strong on the PROBLEM side — the macro case (declining NAEP/PISA, ~18 min/day of K-3 science, the by-age-6 brilliance stereotype, the screen-time crisis, fragmented competitors) is well-sourced, US-specific, and recent, and would convince a skeptic that an early-childhood STEAM gap genuinely exists. The weakness is on the SOLUTION and BUSINESS side, where the paper is materially under-evidenced. Three problems would most hurt it with an investor or partner. (1) Internal inconsistency: the single most important number — US educational-toys market size — appears as three different endpoints (~$13.66B/2030, ~$24.86B/2030, ~$24.6B/2033), the STEM-toys segment differs >5x ($340M vs $1.8B), and women's STEM-workforce share swings 24–35%; these must be reconciled or the paper reads as careless. (2) Borrowed efficacy: every 'it works' claim rests on proxies from the wrong population (Freeman = undergrads, Scully = adults recalling 1990s TV, Tutor CoPilot = human tutors, Heckman = intensive birth-to-five welfare program), with zero evidence on PARI's own story+kit+AI format for ages 3–8. (3) No business case or risk treatment: there is no bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM, unit economics, pricing, churn model, COPPA/AI-safety plan, or moat against well-funded incumbents adding a story/AI layer — and the 'democratizes access' and 'story fixes churn' claims are asserted, not supported. Net: the market-gap thesis is credible and well-defended; the product-fit, defensibility, and commercial-viability arguments need primary or PARI-specific evidence, a reconciled data table, and explicit treatment of AI/child-data risk before the paper would withstand adversarial diligence. Highest-priority fixes: reconcile the conflicting market figures into one sourced table; add bottom-up unit economics + TAM/SAM/SOM; add age-3–8-specific efficacy evidence (or a pilot plan); add a COPPA/AI-safety section; and freshen/date-flag the stalest surveys (esp. the 2019 Junior Achievement 9% figure).

## Introduction: The STEAM Imperative in America

America is building an economy that runs on STEM skills while quietly dismantling the foundation that produces them. This is the defining contradiction of the next decade, and it is most acute in early childhood. The purpose of this white paper is to size that gap precisely and to show why the unmet need sits exactly where PARI STEAM World operates: the early years, before interest and confidence are lost.

### The economy is moving toward STEM. Fast.

STEM is no longer a specialized corner of the labor market; it is the labor market's growth engine. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects STEM occupations will grow 10.4% from 2023 to 2033, nearly triple the 3.6% projected for the rest of the economy (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). The wage premium is just as stark: STEM roles carried a median annual wage of $101,650 in May 2023, more than double the $46,680 median for non-STEM work (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). This is already a foundational pillar of the economy, not a niche — 36 million Americans, roughly a quarter of the workforce, were STEM workers in 2023 (NCSES/NSF, 2024).

| Indicator | STEM | Non-STEM |
|---|---|---|
| Projected job growth, 2023–2033 | 10.4% | 3.6% |
| Median annual wage, May 2023 | $101,650 | $46,680 |

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024

The economic message to families could not be clearer, and parents have heard it: 76% of U.S. parents say they want their child to end up in a STEM-related career (The Toy Association, 2019).

### Yet the foundation is eroding.

Against that surging demand, achievement is moving the wrong direction. The 2024 Nation's Report Card recorded the lowest eighth-grade science performance in over a decade: only 31% of students reached NAEP Proficient, down four points from 2019, while 38% fell below NAEP Basic — the highest share since 2009 (NAGB/NCES, 2025). The decline compounds rather than corrects as students age. By twelfth grade, just 22% were proficient in math, with 45% below NAEP Basic, the largest share ever recorded (NAGB/NCES, 2025). Internationally, U.S. 15-year-olds scored 465 in math on PISA 2022 — below the OECD average, with 25 education systems outscoring them (NCES, 2023).

The root cause sits upstream, in the early grades this paper is concerned with. U.S. K–3 classrooms devote an average of just 18 minutes a day to science, against 89 minutes for English language arts and 57 for math (Horizon Research / 2018 NSSME, 2018). Children are, in effect, not exposed to science during the very window when scientific interest and identity form.

### The central paradox: curiosity without conversion.

The crisis is not a shortage of curiosity. Fully 75% of U.S. Gen Z report interest in STEM — yet only 29% name a STEM role as their first-choice career (Gallup and Walton Family Foundation, 2023). That interest-to-intent gap is the leak in the pipeline, and it is where economic potential drains away. The leak also has a clear equity dimension: 63% of girls express interest in STEM versus 85% of boys, a 22-point gap that appears before career choices are even made (Gallup and Walton Family Foundation, 2023).

So the paradox is fully formed: demand for STEM skills is accelerating and richly rewarded, while achievement falls, early-grade science is crowded out, and the abundant curiosity children start with converts poorly into commitment. The mismatch is structural, and it is widening.

### The demand is large — and the early years are where it concentrates.

This is not a problem in search of a market. The forces above sit on top of a large and fast-growing spend base. The U.S. educational toys market was an estimated $12.19 billion in 2023, growing at a 10.8% CAGR, and the standout signal is that STEM-specific demand within it is the fastest-growing sub-segment at a 15.0% CAGR — STEM is the growth engine, but still under-penetrated (Grand View Research, 2024). The digital layer is an order of magnitude larger: the U.S. EdTech market generated $47.74 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $90.61 billion by 2030, and critically, **preschool is its fastest-growing sector** (Grand View Research, 2024). Households are already paying for enrichment outside school, through a U.S. online private tutoring market of $4.33 billion in 2024 (Grand View Research, 2024).

| U.S. market segment | Size | Growth | Early-years signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Educational toys | $12.19B (2023) | 10.8% CAGR | STEM sub-segment fastest at 15.0% |
| Education technology | $47.74B (2024) | 11.1% CAGR | Preschool fastest-growing sector |
| Online private tutoring | $4.33B (2024) | 11.1% CAGR | Household enrichment spend |

Sources: Grand View Research, 2024

The pattern repeats across every verified layer: the fastest-growing slices are precisely the ones least served for early childhood.

### The thesis: a structural market gap between point solutions and what families need.

The conclusion this paper develops is that the failure is not one of money or of parental will — both are abundant — but of structure. Today's offerings are fragmented into mutually exclusive lanes: kit-only subscriptions, one-off STEM kits, and stand-alone apps. None integrates serialized story, a hands-on physical kit, and an adaptive companion into a single experience, and none centers diverse girl protagonists as role models. A parent who wants hands-on building, narrative motivation, and guided practice must today assemble several disconnected products and bills.

That is the white space, and it sits exactly where the stakes are highest: in the early-childhood window, where identity forms, where instruction is thinnest, and where high-quality intervention earns the highest documented returns. The sections that follow size that gap dimension by dimension — and make the case that closing it is both a commercial opportunity and a national imperative.

## Problem 1 — The Early Identity Crisis: Where Curiosity Erodes

### Children Begin Curious — Then the System Lets That Curiosity Decay

Every child starts as a natural scientist, asking how and why the world works. The American education system, however, does not catch that curiosity at the moment it matters most. By eighth grade, only 28% of US students report a high level of interest and enjoyment in science — down from 38% just five years earlier — with a parallel decline in hands-on scientific inquiry (NAGB/NCES, 2025). The same assessment shows interest converting poorly to mastery: only 31% of eighth graders reached NAEP Proficient in science in 2024, the lowest level in over a decade, while 38% fell below NAEP Basic, the highest share since 2009 (NAGB/NCES, 2025).

This is not a one-grade dip; it is a trajectory. Math scores fell 3 points in grade 4 and 8 points in grade 8 between 2019 and 2024 (NAGB/NCES, 2025), and the erosion compounds rather than corrects with age, bottoming out at just 22% of twelfth graders proficient in math — with 45% below NAEP Basic, the largest such share ever recorded (NAGB/NCES, 2025). A system that lets curiosity leak in elementary and middle school produces a senior class in which fewer than one in four can do grade-level math.

### STEM Identity Forms Before Children Can Articulate It

The decisive insight for early intervention is that a child's self-concept as a "science person" is set long before they could ever describe it. In the landmark study by Bian, Leslie, and Cimpian, gender stereotypes about who is "really, really smart" were measurable in girls by **age 6 — and were not present at age 5** — and already shaped which activities girls chose to avoid (Science, 2017). Identity foreclosure begins, in other words, in kindergarten.

Achievement gaps follow the same precocious timeline. Racial and ethnic disparities in advanced (above-90th-percentile) science and math achievement are visible at kindergarten entry and remain stable or widen through fifth grade (Educational Researcher, 2023):

| Group | Advanced science/math achievement at kindergarten |
|---|---|
| White students | ~13%–16% |
| Black or Hispanic students | ~3%–4% |

*(Educational Researcher, 2023; population-based ECLS-K cohort of 10,922 children)*

And the foundation laid in these years anchors everything that follows: across six US longitudinal datasets, school-entry (kindergarten) math skill was the single strongest predictor of later achievement in **both** math and reading — ahead of early reading and attention skills (Developmental Psychology, 2007). The window in which STEM trajectories are decided opens before formal science instruction typically begins.

### The Early Window Is Being Missed

If identity forms first, the system's response is to invest in it last. US self-contained elementary classrooms devote an average of just **18 minutes a day to science in grades K–3** — versus 89 minutes for English language arts and 57 for math — rising only to 27 minutes a day in grades 4–6 (Horizon Research, 2019).

| Subject | Avg. minutes/day, grades K–3 | Avg. minutes/day, grades 4–6 |
|---|---|---|
| Reading / language arts | 89 | 82 |
| Mathematics | 57 | 63 |
| **Science** | **18** | **27** |

*(Horizon Research / 2018 NSSME+, 2019)*

Worse, that minimal time is sporadic. Science is taught every day of the week, every week of the year in only **17% of K–3 classes** (and 35% of grades 4–6), whereas math is taught on most or all school days in nearly every class (Horizon Research, 2019). When science is taught, it is often delivered by educators who feel unequipped: only **31% of self-contained elementary teachers feel "very well prepared" to teach science**, against 77% for reading and 73% for math, and only about 3% hold a degree in a science field (Horizon Research, 2019). The developmental window most open to wonder receives the least, most inconsistent, and least confidently delivered instruction in the building.

### Equity Gaps Are Baked In at the Starting Line

Because identity and achievement gaps appear at kindergarten entry, the early window is also the most equitable — and currently the most neglected — point of intervention. The gendered "brilliance" stereotype that emerges by age 6 (Science, 2017) compounds over time: the share of girls who draw a female scientist falls from about 70% among 6-year-olds to roughly 25% among 16-year-olds (Northwestern/Child Development, 2018). By age 15, US science literacy is middling rather than leading — 499 on PISA 2022, with 9 systems scoring higher (NCES, 2024) — and by adulthood women make up only about 26% of the US STEM workforce (AAUW, 2023). A gender gap in eighth-grade NAEP science even re-emerged in 2024, with boys outscoring girls by a statistically significant margin after no significant gap in 2019 (NAGB, 2025). None of these endpoints is set at the endpoint; each is seeded at the start.

### Why This Is the Highest-Leverage Moment

The economics confirm what the developmental science implies. High-quality birth-to-five programs for disadvantaged US children have delivered returns of about **13% per year** (benefit-cost ratio 6.3), exceeding the 7%–10% established for preschool-only programs (Heckman Equation, 2017). The early window is therefore not only where curiosity is most malleable and gaps most preventable — it is where every dollar of intervention works hardest. The American system creates STEM winners and losers before children can read, then spends 18 minutes a day on the subject that decides the outcome. Closing the early STEAM gap means meeting children in exactly this window — before interest erodes, before stereotypes harden, and before the identity crisis becomes a lifelong trajectory.

## Problem 2 — The Representation Gap: Why Girls Opt Out

### A Pipeline That Leaks Before It Fills

Women are roughly half of the U.S. workforce, yet they remain a persistent minority in the fields that define the modern economy. Of the 36 million STEM workers in the United States in 2023, only 35% were women, and women hold just about 27% of core science and engineering occupations (NSF/NCSES, 2026). The shortfall is sharpest in precisely the disciplines PARI STEAM World centers. Women make up only about 16% of engineers and roughly 26% of computer and mathematical scientists (NSF/NCSES, 2023).

| STEM segment | Share of women | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Overall STEM workforce (2023) | 35% | NSF/NCSES, 2026 |
| Core science & engineering occupations | ~27% | NSF/NCSES, 2026 |
| Engineers | ~16% | NSF/NCSES, 2023 |
| Computer & mathematical scientists | ~26% | NSF/NCSES, 2023 |

Critically, this is not a question of ability or access to credentials. Women earn roughly half of all science and engineering bachelor's degrees, yet that near-parity collapses to about 24% of engineering and 22% of computing degrees (NSF/NCSES, 2024). A pipeline that begins at parity and ends at a quarter is leaking somewhere upstream — and the evidence points to early childhood.

### The Gap Opens at Age 6

The most rigorous developmental research locates the origin point with unusual precision. In a landmark study published in *Science*, by age 6 U.S. girls become less likely than boys to associate being "really, really smart" with their own gender, and begin actively avoiding activities described as being for "really, really smart" children — a gap that was not present at age 5 (Bian, Leslie & Cimpian, 2017). The "brilliance equals male" stereotype, in other words, is absent in kindergarten and measurable by first grade.

That early belief hardens with every additional year of schooling. A meta-analysis of 78 U.S. "Draw-A-Scientist" studies spanning five decades and more than 20,000 children found real cultural progress — the share drawing a female scientist rose from under 1% in 1966–1977 to 28% in 1985–2016 — yet the association of science with men still strengthens sharply with age. About 70% of 6-year-old girls draw a woman scientist, but only roughly 25% of 16-year-old girls do (Miller, Nolla, Eagly & Uttal, 2018).

| Age | Girls drawing a female scientist |
|---|---|
| 6 years | ~70% |
| 16 years | ~25% |

The attitudinal consequences are visible by adolescence. In a national survey of U.S. teens ages 13–17, only 9% of girls expressed interest in a STEM career, down from 11%, versus 27% for boys (Junior Achievement USA, 2019). Confidence erodes in parallel: the share of U.S. girls who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% in 2017 to 59% in 2024 (ROX, 2024), with the steepest collapse in self-belief occurring in the early grades. By the time these girls reach eighth grade, the gap shows up in achievement itself — a statistically significant gender gap in NAEP science re-emerged in 2024, with boys outscoring girls after no measurable gap in 2019 (NAGB, 2025).

### Why Role Models Are the Decisive Lever

If the stereotype is learned, it can be unlearned — and the most rigorously evidenced countermeasure is exposure to relatable role models. The causal U.S. evidence is striking in its magnitude:

| Intervention | Measured effect | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Single guest talk by a woman economist | Women majoring in economics rose 8 points (9% → 17%) | Porter & Serra, via J-PAL, 2024 |
| Woman professor in intro math/science | Closed ~75% of the gender grade gap | Carrell, Page & West, via J-PAL, 2024 |
| Same-gender role-model exposure | Raised high-performing women's choice of underrepresented STEM majors by up to 26 points | Kofoed & McGovney, via J-PAL, 2024 |

Fictional role models work too, and their effects track real behavior, not just attitudes. In the Geena Davis Institute's "Scully Effect" study of roughly 2,000 U.S. women, 63% of those working in STEM named the fictional scientist Dana Scully a personal role model, and medium-to-heavy female viewers of *The X-Files* were 50% more likely to have actually worked in a STEM field than non- or light viewers (24% vs. 16%) (Geena Davis Institute, 2018). Demand for such representation is explicit: 71% of surveyed audiences say female STEM representation on-screen is important, up 20 points since 2018 (Geena Davis Institute, 2024).

### The Supply Deficit: Where Are the Girl Scientists?

Here the market fails the moment most decisively. Across 15 years of top U.S. television and film (2007–2022), women were just 37% of STEM characters in 2007–2017 and 38% in 2018–2022. The picture is bleaker still in the highest-leverage fields: female engineers were only 13% of on-screen STEM roles and computer scientists only 15% in 2018–2022 (Geena Davis Institute, 2024). The very stereotype that takes hold at age 6 is reinforced by media that overwhelmingly shows girls a male scientist.

The result is a precisely defined white space. The gender gap is seeded by a stereotype that emerges by age 6 and strengthens through adolescence; the proven antidote — relatable, same-gender role models — produces 8- to 26-point shifts in girls' STEM persistence; yet girls almost never see female STEM protagonists, even as more than seven in ten audiences say they want them. By placing two diverse girl protagonists, PARI and Sarala, at the center of serialized science adventures during the identity-forming early-childhood window, PARI STEAM World intervenes before the stereotype hardens — converting a documented, unmet, and explicitly demanded need into a defensible market position.

## Problem 3 — The Screen-Time Paradox and the Hands-On Deficit

### Screens now begin in infancy and far outrun the guidance

American childhood has been quietly rewired. Screen exposure no longer starts in the elementary years; it starts before a child can speak. The 2025 Common Sense Census finds that US children under age 2 average about 1 hour 3 minutes of screen media per day, ages 2–4 average roughly 2 hours 8 minutes, and ages 5–8 average roughly 3 hours 28 minutes (Common Sense Media, 2025). Personal device ownership has pushed just as deep: 40% of US children have their own tablet by age 2, and nearly 1 in 4 have a personal cellphone by age 8 (Common Sense Media, 2025). Even where total time has plateaued at about 2.5 hours a day for kids 8 and under, the composition has shifted toward the most immersive formats — gaming time surged 65% over four years (Common Sense Media, 2025).

This reality sits in direct tension with the standard of care. The American Academy of Pediatrics discourages screen media other than video chatting for children younger than 18 months, and recommends limiting screen use to 1 hour per day of high-quality programming for ages 2–5, reserving time for free play, sleep, and physical activity (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2016). The gap between the recommended ceiling and observed reality is not marginal — for the 2–4 band, typical use is roughly double the AAP's one-hour guideline.

| Age band | Average daily screen time | AAP guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Under 2 | ~1 hr 3 min (Common Sense Media, 2025) | Discouraged except video chat (AAP, 2016) |
| 2–4 | ~2 hr 8 min (Common Sense Media, 2025) | ≤1 hr/day high-quality programming (AAP, 2016) |
| 5–8 | ~3 hr 28 min (Common Sense Media, 2025) | Consistent limits, prioritize free play (AAP, 2016) |

### Parental anxiety is mainstream, and the policy signal is federal

Concern about all of this is not a fringe position held by a worried minority — it is the parental mainstream. Pew Research Center's October 2025 survey of parents of children 12 and under found that 42% feel they could be doing a better job managing their child's screen time, and 80% say social media's harms for kids outweigh its benefits (Pew Research Center, 2025). Broader census data corroborate the unease: roughly 75–80% of US parents express concern about screen media, including its mental-health effects, even as children 8 and under average about 2.5 hours of daily screen time (Common Sense Media, 2025).

Government has elevated this from private worry to public-health priority. The 2023 US Surgeon General's Advisory documents that up to 95% of youth ages 13–17 use a social media platform — more than a third "almost constantly" — and that nearly 40% of children ages 8–12 already use social media (US Surgeon General, 2023). The Advisory's headline finding is the stakes: adolescents who spend more than 3 hours per day on social media face roughly double the risk of poor mental-health outcomes, including depression and anxiety symptoms (US Surgeon General, 2023). Peer-reviewed US evidence points the same direction; in a national population-based study, 14–17-year-old high screen users (7+ hours/day) were more than twice as likely to have been diagnosed with depression (RR 2.39) or anxiety (RR 2.26) than low users (Preventive Medicine Reports, 2018). When the nation's chief physician, the leading pediatric body, and independent researchers converge, parents are right to read it as a signal to act.

### The unmet demand: hands-on, offline — but still modern

The flip side of this anxiety is concrete, monetizable demand for a healthier alternative. It is the same demand documented across parent-attitude research: 78% of US parents want more toys that help their children develop skills like creativity and problem-solving, and the Toy Association now flags "screen-free play" and open-ended, maker-style kits as leading purchase trends (The Toy Association, 2025). This is not nostalgia for low-tech play; it is a preference for active, developmental engagement over passive consumption. Parents already treat play as serious developmental infrastructure — 94% say toys play a significant role in their child's development and 91% emphasize the importance of educational toys (The Toy Association, 2023).

The market is sizing up around exactly this preference. The US educational toys market was estimated at about $12.19 billion in 2023, with hands-on STEM/learning cited as a primary growth driver, and the STEM-specific demand inside that category is its fastest-growing sub-segment at a 15.0% CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024). The US STEM toys segment specifically was about $1.8 billion in 2024, accounting for roughly 85% of the North American STEM toys market (Grand View Research; Global Market Insights, 2024). Crucially, parents will pay premium, recurring prices for curated, developmentally-staged hands-on experiences: Lovevery's lifetime sales per customer reached $692.38 after 24 months, more than double KiwiCo's and Little Passports' (Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021).

The strategic insight is that the alternative parents want cannot simply be "less." The same families anxious about screens live in a digital world — 40% of toddlers have a tablet by age 2 and 0–8s average 2.5 hours of screen time daily (Common Sense Media, 2025) — so a credible offering must feel modern and meet children where they are, not retreat from technology entirely. A purely analog product reads as a step backward; a purely digital one is more of the problem. The white space is a screen-balanced, tactile experience: hands-on building and creativity as the spine, with technology used deliberately and in moderation rather than as the default mode of engagement.

### Why this is a defensible position, not a wish

The case rests on two independent signals pointing at the same gap. The demand signal is parental anxiety — federal and pediatric authorities urging less screen time, with 80% of parents agreeing the harms outweigh the benefits (Pew Research Center, 2025) and three-quarters expressing concern (Common Sense Media, 2025). The supply signal is willingness to pay — a roughly $12-billion-and-growing US educational-toy market (Grand View Research, 2024), a STEM sub-segment compounding at 15.0% (Grand View Research, 2024), and proven premium recurring spend (Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021). Parents are not merely worried; they are already spending, and they are explicitly asking for skill-building, screen-free play (The Toy Association, 2025). A tactile, STEAM-focused, screen-balanced early-learning experience converts that documented anxiety and stated demand into a value proposition that pediatric and federal guidance actively endorse — healthy, offline, creativity-building learning that still feels current to a digital-native child.

## Market Gap Analysis: A Fragmented Landscape of Point Solutions

The US market for children's learning products is large, growing, and unambiguously underserved at the level that matters most: integration. The US educational toys market was valued at roughly $11.1 billion in 2024 and is projected to more than double to about $24.6 billion by 2033, a 9.2% CAGR (Custom Market Insights, 2024). Yet the offerings competing for that spend are siloed by format. Physical-kit subscriptions, one-off app-plus-pieces systems, and screen-based apps each occupy a separate lane, and almost none combine serialized story, a hands-on kit, and an AI companion in a single connected product. The result is a market full of competent point solutions and empty of integrated ones.

### Every Major Player Solves Only One Slice

Profiling the incumbents most available to US parents makes the fragmentation concrete. KiwiCo is a physical-kit subscription with no app or narrative spine. Lovevery sells a premium Montessori toy subscription, again kit-only. MEL Science pairs science kits with companion app/AR content but no serialized characters. Osmo is an app-plus-physical-pieces system tethered to a tablet and sold as a one-off. Khan Academy Kids is a pure, free app with no physical component (Groupon, 2025; Lovevery, 2025; MEL Science / Khan Academy / PlayOsmo, 2025).

| Player | Offering | Model | Price | Story? | Kit? | AI? | Diverse girl role models? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KiwiCo | STEM craft crates | Subscription | $23.95/mo core; $32.95/mo Maker & Eureka | No | Yes | No | No |
| Lovevery | Montessori play kits | Subscription | ~$40/mo effective ($80/2mo baby; $120/3mo toddler) | No | Yes | No | No |
| MEL Science | Science kits + app/AR | Subscription | $34.90/mo ($25.90/mo annual) | No | Yes | Partial (app/AR, no characters) | No |
| Osmo | App + physical pieces | One-time purchase | ~$90 list (Genius Starter Kit) | No | Yes | App-tethered, not adaptive | No |
| Khan Academy Kids | Learning app | Free | $0 | No | No | No | No |
| **Integrated model (PARI STEAM World)** | **Serialized story + DIY kit + AI companion** | **Subscription ecosystem** | **—** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes (parent-governed)** | **Yes** |

Sources: Groupon (2025); Lovevery (2025); MEL Science / Khan Academy / PlayOsmo (2025).

Read across the columns and the gap is structural, not incidental. No incumbent owns more than two of the four dimensions, and none centers diverse girl protagonists as role models. A parent who wants hands-on building, screen-based reinforcement, narrative motivation, and adaptive guidance must stitch together several separate products and several separate bills to assemble what should be one experience.

### Fragmentation Forces Parents to Be Integrators

This stitching problem is not theoretical. Each format solves one slice, so coverage requires assembly: a kit subscription for the hands, an app for the screen, and nothing at all for the narrative motivation or the personalized guidance that sustains engagement between deliveries. That burden lands precisely on an audience that has already gone digital. US children ages 0-8 average about 2.5 hours of screen time per day, and 40% have a tablet by age 2 (Common Sense Media, 2025), which means a blended physical-plus-digital experience would meet kids where they already are rather than forcing parents to choose between a craft box and a screen.

The single-format model also carries a documented retention penalty. McKinsey's survey of more than 5,000 US consumers found that over one-third of subscription consumers cancel within three months and more than half within six, with nearly 40% ultimately canceling; for curation and access boxes, the most-cited reason is "not getting value for the money" at 29% (McKinsey & Company, 2018). Independent benchmarks put subscription-box monthly churn commonly at 10-15% (SubJolt, 2026). A disconnected craft shipped each month has little structural defense against that churn. A serialized story and a persistent companion that continue between shipments do — engagement is the spine that single-format incumbents lack.

### The Sharpest White Space: Integration Plus Representation

The fragmentation gap is sharpened by a second one that no incumbent addresses: representation. The role-model deficit is acute and quantified. Women make up only 27% of the US STEM workforce despite being 48% of all workers (U.S. Census Bureau, 2021). Teen girls' interest in a STEM career has fallen to 9%, versus 27% for boys (Junior Achievement USA, 2019), and the share of US girls who believe they are good at math and science dropped from 73% in 2017 to 59% (ROX, 2024). These are confidence and identity gaps that disconnected kits and content-neutral apps are not designed to close.

The two gaps intersect at an unoccupied position. No major US incumbent integrates serialized storytelling, a hands-on kit, and an adaptive AI companion in one product, and none centers diverse girl heroes inside that integration. The market is split into mutually exclusive formats, churn punishes the single-format model, and a documented social need for girl-forward STEM representation goes unmet. The white space is therefore not a marginally better kit or a slightly cheaper app — it is the integrated story + kit + AI ecosystem with diverse girl protagonists at its center, in a large (~$11.1B, 9.2% CAGR) but siloed US market (Custom Market Insights, 2024) where the audience is already primed for a blended experience and where no competitor occupies the intersection.

The US children's learning economy is not a single market but a stack of segments, each growing well above GDP. Two signals deserve emphasis. First, **early childhood is where the momentum is**: within US EdTech, K-12 is the largest sector but **preschool is the fastest-growing** through 2030 (Grand View Research, 2024) — precisely the under-served age band PARI targets. Second, **AI-driven personalization is the steepest curve in the entire stack**, with US AI-in-education compounding at 31.2% to $8.84 billion by 2030 (Grand View Research, 2024), validating PARI's AI-companion layer as a tailwind rather than a gamble.

### TAM: The Total Spend Pool

We define the total addressable market as US household and institutional spend that an integrated early-STEAM ecosystem can plausibly touch. The most direct envelope is the US educational toys market — $12.19 billion in 2023, growing at 10.8% (Grand View Research, 2024) — sitting alongside adjacent enrichment budgets parents already pay into: the **US total private tutoring market of $39.6 billion in 2024** (Global Industry Analysts, 2024) and the **$47.74 billion US EdTech market** (Grand View Research, 2024). Critically, demand inside the educational-toys category is not evenly distributed: **STEM-toy demand is the fastest-growing sub-segment at a 15.0% CAGR, outpacing the 10.8% category average** (Grand View Research, 2024). STEM is the growth engine, yet remains under-penetrated relative to total educational-toy spend — the white space PARI is built to capture.

### SAM: The STEM-Specific Slice We Serve

The serviceable addressable market narrows to dedicated, hands-on STEM products and the digital learning that complements them. Here the verified numbers are notably smaller than headline figures suggest, which is exactly why the opportunity is real. Pure-play STEM toys are still a niche: the **North America STEM toys market was $425.9 million in 2024**, rising to $629.2 million by 2030 (Grand View Research, 2024), and because the **US holds roughly 80% of that North American market, the US STEM-toys segment is on the order of $340 million in 2024** (Grand View Research, 2024). That a category whose underlying demand grows at 15.0% has only matured to a few hundred million dollars signals room to convert general educational-toy and tutoring buyers into dedicated STEM buyers — rather than a saturated field to fight over.

Layered on top is genuine, durable willingness to pay for **supplemental digital learning**: the US online private tutoring market nearly doubles from $4.33 billion (2024) to $8.09 billion (2030) at 11.1% (Grand View Research, 2025), the same household enrichment budget a subscription STEAM product competes for.

### Parent Willingness-to-Pay: The Demand Engine Beneath the Numbers

Market size means little without confirmed willingness to pay, and the parent-attitudes evidence is unambiguous. **76% of US parents want their child to end up in a STEM-related career** (The Toy Association, 2019), and **94% say toys play a significant role in their child's development while 78% want more toys that build creativity and problem-solving** (The Toy Association, 2023) — demand for developmental, hands-on play over passive entertainment. That preference converts to real, recurring dollars: in the hands-on educational-subscription category, **Lovevery's lifetime sales per customer reached $692.38 after 24 months — more than double KiwiCo's and Little Passports'** (Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021), proof that US parents will pay premium, recurring prices for curated, developmentally-staged STEAM experiences.

The spend is steep but unequal: **high-income US families spend roughly $8,900 per child per year on enrichment versus about $1,300 for the lowest-income quintile — a gap that widened from ~4x to ~7x** (The Hamilton Project, 2018). Even mainstream households budget meaningfully, with back-to-school spending projected at about **$886 per household in 2025** (Empower, 2025). The willingness exists across the income spectrum; affordable, high-quality early STEAM is the lever that broadens access beyond the affluent top quintile.

### SOM: A Realistic Beachhead

The serviceable obtainable market is the share PARI can capture in its early years by owning an unoccupied position — integrated story, kit, and AI companion with diverse girl protagonists — inside a US STEM-toys niche of roughly $340 million (Grand View Research, 2024) that is expanding off a 15.0% demand CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024), while drawing spillover from the multi-billion-dollar US educational-toys ($12.19B), tutoring ($39.6B), and preschool-led EdTech pools. The strategic logic is consistent across every verified layer: **the fastest-growing slices of the US education economy — STEM demand (15.0%), preschool EdTech, and AI-in-education (31.2%) — are precisely the ones least served for early childhood today.** That mismatch between where demand is accelerating and where dedicated products exist is the market opportunity PARI STEAM World is positioned to convert.

## The Evidence Base: Why Story + Hands-On + Representation Works

The PARI STEAM World model rests on four pedagogical pillars — narrative learning, hands-on making, diverse role models, and a carefully bounded AI companion. None of these is a marketing intuition. Each is independently validated by rigorous US research, and the most defensible design choice is to fuse them while keeping the experience physical-first and screen-balanced. The evidence below makes that case to a skeptical reader and pre-empts the obvious objection: that this is "just another screen."

### Hands-on beats passive: the strongest causal evidence in STEM pedagogy

The largest and most-cited body of causal evidence in STEM education points one direction — students learn more by doing than by watching. Freeman et al.'s landmark meta-analysis of 225 undergraduate STEM courses found that active, hands-on learning raised exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations (about half a letter grade), while students in traditional lecture courses were roughly 1.5x more likely to fail (failure odds ratio 1.95) (PNAS, 2014). The study is university-level, so it is directional rather than dispositive for early childhood, but it is the most robust available foundation for the maker, project-based, and DIY-kit approach that sits at the center of this concept. Doing is not a "nice to have"; it is the instructional mechanism with the strongest measured returns.

### Representation changes aspiration — and real behavior

The case for diverse, relatable STEM characters is unusually well documented because it links fiction to real-world outcomes, not just attitudes. In the Geena Davis Institute "Scully Effect" study of roughly 2,000 US women aged 25+, 63% of women working in STEM named the fictional scientist Dana Scully as a personal role model, 91% saw her as a role model for girls and women, and 63% said she increased their confidence to excel in a male-dominated profession (Geena Davis Institute, 2018). Crucially, identification tracked with behavior: medium-to-heavy female viewers of *The X-Files* were 50% more likely to have actually worked in a STEM field than non/light viewers (24% vs 16%) (Geena Davis Institute, 2018).

The need this addresses is acute and worsening. A national school-based survey of 17,502 US girls in grades 5–12 found the share who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% (2017) to 59% (2024), even as stated interest in a STEM career rose to 55% from 45% — a widening interest-versus-confidence gap (ROX Girls' Index, 2024). The collapse is sharpest in the early grades: among 5th–6th graders, the share saying they don't believe they are smart enough for their dream job jumped from 23% to 52% (ROX Girls' Index, 2024). And the stereotype forms even earlier — by age 6, US girls become less likely than boys to associate being "really, really smart" with their own gender, a gap not present at age 5 (Bian, Leslie & Cimpian, 2017). Representation-rich storytelling is the evidence-backed countermeasure, applied in precisely the window where confidence is most malleable.

### AI as a supervised co-pilot — not an unsupervised babysitter

AI belongs in the model, but only as a parent-governed assist layer. The distinction is what the data supports. Stanford's randomized controlled trial of Tutor CoPilot (900 tutors, ~1,800 K-12 students in a majority-Hispanic Title I district) found students of AI-assisted tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics, rising to 9 points for students of the lowest-rated tutors (Stanford, 2024) — gains that appear when AI *augments* human guidance.

The flip side is a trust gap the design must respect. A quarter of US public-school teachers say AI tools do more harm than good in K-12, versus just 6% who say more good than harm (Pew Research Center, 2024). And 72% of US teens have used an AI companion, 52% regularly, with about one-third finding AI conversations as satisfying as or more than those with real friends (Common Sense Media, 2025). That is the precise risk a parent-trusted, transparent, supervised AI layer is built to avoid.

### Pre-empting the "just another screen" objection

The strongest defense of a physical-first design is the market reality it answers. US children are already saturated with screens — ages 5–8 average about 3 hours 28 minutes of screen media a day, gaming among kids 8-and-under surged 65% in four years, and 40% have a tablet by age 2 (Common Sense Media, 2025) — all far above the AAP's guidance of no screens under 18 months and one hour of high-quality programming for ages 2–5 (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2016). Parents feel the strain: 42% say they could do better managing screen time, and 80% say social media does more harm than good for kids (Pew Research Center, 2025).

That anxiety is monetizable demand for the opposite of another screen. 78% of US parents want more toys that build creativity and problem-solving, with screen-free, maker-style play flagged as a leading trend (The Toy Association, 2025), and 94% say toys play a significant role in development (The Toy Association, 2023).

| Design pillar | Evidence the dossier supplies | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Hands-on / maker first | +0.47 SD exam gain; lecture failure OR 1.95 | PNAS, 2014 |
| Diverse role models | 63% of women in STEM cite a fictional role model; 24% vs 16% real-career effect | Geena Davis Institute, 2018 |
| AI as supervised co-pilot | +4 to +9 pp math mastery when AI augments tutors | Stanford, 2024 |
| Screen-balanced by design | Ages 5–8 average 3h28m/day; 78% of parents want creativity-building toys | Common Sense Media, 2025; The Toy Association, 2025 |

The conclusion is not that screens are banned, but that the screen is the smallest, most supervised part of an experience anchored in story and physical making. PARI STEAM World is engineered to be the healthy, hands-on alternative that pediatric guidance endorses and parents are actively shopping for — story to motivate, kits to build, representation to inspire, and AI kept on a short, transparent leash.

## Solution Fit: How PARI STEAM World Closes the Gap

The preceding sections documented six interlocking failures in America's early-STEAM landscape: science is crowded out of the early grades, STEM identity hardens before children can read, girls disengage as gender stereotypes take hold, parents are anxious but underserved, screens dominate young children's time, and the existing market is fragmented into single-format products. PARI STEAM World is architected as a direct, point-by-point response. Its four pillars are not four features bolted together; each maps onto a specific, evidence-documented gap. This section makes that mapping explicit and positions the concept against the evidence — without claiming outcomes the company has not yet measured.

### The Four Pillars, and Why Each Exists

**Pillar 1 — Serialized storytelling with girl protagonists (PARI & Sarala).** Story is the engagement spine and the representation vehicle. The strongest US "see it, be it" evidence — the Scully Effect study — found that 63% of US women working in STEM named a single fictional scientist as their personal role model, and that medium/heavy female viewers were 50% more likely to have actually worked in STEM (24% vs 16%) (Geena Davis Institute, 2018). Narrative also addresses the documented confidence collapse: the share of US girls who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% to 59% (ROX, 2024). And it is a structural retention mechanism in a market where more than one-third of subscribers cancel within three months (McKinsey, 2018).

**Pillar 2 — DIY hands-on STEM kits.** The kits operationalize "doing over listening," the instructional approach with the strongest causal evidence: active learning raised exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations and lecture-only students were ~1.5x more likely to fail (PNAS / Freeman et al., 2014). Tactile, screen-light kits also meet documented parent demand — 78% of US parents want more toys that build creativity and problem-solving (The Toy Association, 2025) — amid 75-80% parental concern about screens (Common Sense Media, 2025).

**Pillar 3 — AI learning companion.** The companion is designed as a supervised, parent-governed assist layer, not an unsupervised screen substitute. This reflects the double-edged AI evidence: human-plus-AI tutoring lifted math mastery by 4-9 percentage points (Stanford, 2024), yet 25% of US teachers say AI does more harm than good (Pew, 2024) and 72% of teens already use AI companions, 52% regularly (Common Sense Media, 2025). It also rides the fastest-growing US education layer — AI in education compounding at 31.2% CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024).

**Pillar 4 — Early-childhood start with diverse role models.** The concept targets the identity-forming window because that is where the leverage is. Gender stereotypes about who is "really, really smart" are measurable by age 6 and absent at age 5 (Bian, Leslie & Cimpian, 2017), advanced achievement gaps exist at kindergarten entry (Morgan et al., 2023), and high-quality early-childhood programs return ~13% per year (Heckman, 2017) — yet K-3 classrooms devote just ~18 minutes a day to science (Horizon Research, 2018).

### Gap → Evidence → PARI Solution

| Documented gap | Anchoring evidence | PARI pillar that addresses it |
|---|---|---|
| Science crowded out of early grades | ~18 min/day on science in K-3 vs 89 for ELA, 57 for math; daily all year in only 17% of classes (Horizon Research, 2018/2019) | Early-childhood start + DIY kits deliver consistent at-home STEM exposure |
| STEM identity forms before school | Gender "brilliance" stereotype emerges by age 6; achievement gaps present at kindergarten (Bian et al., 2017; Morgan et al., 2023) | Early-childhood start during the malleable window |
| Girls disengage; confidence falls | Good-at-math/science 73%→59%; teen girls' STEM-career interest 9% vs boys 27% (ROX, 2024; Junior Achievement, 2019) | Girl protagonists PARI & Sarala as role models |
| Role models missing from media | Women only 37-38% of on-screen STEM characters, engineers just 13%; 71% want more representation (Geena Davis Institute, 2024) | Serialized storytelling centered on diverse girl heroes |
| Passive instruction underperforms | Active learning +0.47 SD; failure odds ratio 1.95 (PNAS / Freeman et al., 2014) | Hands-on DIY kits (project-based doing) |
| Excessive screen time; parent worry | 75-80% of parents concerned; 78% want creativity/problem-solving toys (Common Sense Media, 2025; Toy Association, 2025) | Screen-light kits + supervised, bounded AI |
| AI distrust caps adoption | 25% of teachers say AI does more harm than good; gains only when AI augments humans (+4-9 pp) (Pew, 2024; Stanford, 2024) | AI as a transparent, parent-governed co-pilot |
| Market is fragmented by format | No US incumbent integrates story + kit + AI; >⅓ of subscribers cancel within 3 months (Competitive analysis; McKinsey, 2018) | All four pillars in one connected ecosystem |
| Interest converts poorly to intent | 75% of Gen Z interested in STEM, only 29% name it first-choice career (Gallup/Walton, 2023) | Story-driven motivation sustained from early childhood |

### Why the Integration, Not Just the Parts, Is the Fit

Each pillar answers a gap, but the concept's differentiated position is the combination. The competitive analysis shows the US market is split into mutually exclusive lanes — KiwiCo and Lovevery are kit-only, MEL Science is kit-plus-app, Osmo is app-plus-pieces, Khan Academy Kids is a free app — and no major incumbent centers diverse girl protagonists inside an integrated story-kit-AI format. That fragmentation forces parents to stitch together several products and bills, and it leaves single-format subscriptions exposed to 10-15% monthly churn (SubJolt, 2026). PARI STEAM World's thesis is that a serialized narrative and persistent companion supply the engagement spine that disconnected monthly kits lack.

The demand-side conditions also align. The audience is already blended-ready — children 0-8 average ~2.5 hours of daily screen time and 40% have a tablet by age 2 (Common Sense Media, 2025) — so a physical-plus-digital format meets families where they are rather than fighting their habits. Parents are primed to pay: the US educational-toys market runs ~$12.19B with STEM the fastest-growing sub-segment at 15.0% CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024), preschool is the fastest-growing EdTech sector (Grand View Research, 2024), and premium recurring spend is proven (Lovevery's $692 lifetime value per customer) (Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021).

A deliberate note on scope: PARI STEAM World is positioning a concept, not reporting trial results. The cited effect sizes — Freeman's 0.47 SD, Tutor CoPilot's 4-9 points, the Scully Effect's 50% differential — establish that each design choice rests on mechanisms shown to work in US contexts, not that PARI has yet produced equivalent outcomes. The claim made here is one of fit: the product's four pillars map cleanly, gap by gap, onto the documented failures of America's early-STEAM system, and their integration occupies a white space no current US incumbent holds.

## Validating Demand: The PARI Parent Survey as Primary Research

Every preceding section of this white paper rests on secondary evidence: national assessments, peer-reviewed developmental studies, federal labor projections, and third-party market sizing. That body of evidence is unusually consistent, but it is, by definition, about the market in aggregate, not about PARI STEAM World specifically. The PARI Parent Survey is the company's primary-research layer, designed to convert documented macro-gaps into product-level demand signal. It tests, against real parents, whether the behaviors, anxieties, and willingness-to-pay implied by the dossier actually attach to this concept, this format, and this price.

### From documented gaps to testable hypotheses

The survey is structured so that each section interrogates a specific, pre-registered hypothesis drawn directly from the secondary record. The intent is not to ask parents whether they like the idea, but to triangulate stated demand against the independent benchmarks already established in this paper.

| Section | Hypothesis under test | Dossier anchor it validates against |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Family profile** | The reachable audience skews toward the early-childhood, education-engaged household. | Preschool is the fastest-growing US EdTech sector (Grand View Research, 2024). |
| **B. How children spend time** | Screen time is high and parents are dissatisfied with it. | Kids 0-8 average ~2.5 hours of screen time daily (Common Sense Media, 2025). |
| **C. Parent concerns** | Future-skills anxiety is real and STEM-linked. | 76% of parents want a STEM career for their child (The Toy Association, 2019). |
| **D. STEM attitudes** | Parents rate STEM highly yet see latent, unconverted curiosity in their child. | 75% of Gen Z report STEM interest; only 29% name it a first-choice career (Gallup/Walton, 2023). |
| **E. Purchase behavior** | Parents already spend on educational products, including STEM kits. | US educational toys market ~$12.19B, STEM the fastest sub-segment at 15.0% CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024). |
| **F. Concept test** | The integrated story + kit + AI concept has standalone appeal. | No incumbent integrates all three (Custom Market Insights / competitive analysis, 2024). |
| **G. DIY kit demand** | Specific kit concepts command differentiated interest. | 78% of parents want more creativity/problem-solving toys (The Toy Association, 2025). |
| **H. Role-model validation** | Parents value seeing all genders as scientists. | Female role-model exposure lifts girls' STEM persistence 8-26 pts (J-PAL, 2024). |
| **I. Pricing** | A premium, recurring price is acceptable for a complete experience. | Lovevery lifetime value reached $692.38 per customer (Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021). |
| **J. Open-ended** | Parents will articulate the unmet need in their own words. | Awareness gap: 89% think their child is on track (Gallup/Learning Heroes, 2023). |

### What each cluster is built to prove

**Sections A-C establish the problem in the household.** Section B measures recreational screen time and satisfaction, testing whether the parental ambivalence documented nationally (~75-80% express concern about screen media, Common Sense Media, 2025) shows up among prospective buyers and creates appetite for a screen-light alternative. Section C surfaces the worry that the "B-flation" research shows is latent but easily activated once parents learn the truth (Gallup/Learning Heroes, 2023). These sections exist to confirm that the demand we infer from secondary data is felt, not merely statistical.

**Sections D-E translate concern into category behavior.** Section D separates parental valuation of STEM from the child's observed curiosity, the same interest-to-intent gap that defines the national opportunity (Gallup/Walton, 2023). Section E quantifies actual annual spend and prior STEM-kit purchase, grounding willingness-to-pay in revealed behavior rather than aspiration, and benchmarking it against the ~$12.19B US educational-toys category where STEM is the fastest-growing slice at a 15.0% CAGR (Grand View Research, 2024).

**Sections F-G are the core concept and product test.** Section F scores appeal of the integrated story + kit + AI model on a 1-10 scale and isolates which element drives interest and which raises concern, directly probing the white space no incumbent occupies (competitive analysis, 2024). Section G rates eight discrete kit concepts on a 1-5 scale, producing a demand-ranked roadmap rather than a single yes/no, and operationalizing the documented appetite for hands-on, creativity-building play (78% of parents, The Toy Association, 2025).

**Section H validates the differentiator.** It tests whether parents endorse diverse girl protagonists as role models, the lever with the strongest causal evidence in the dossier: female role-model exposure raises girls' STEM persistence by 8 to 26 percentage points (J-PAL, 2024), and character identification tracks real career behavior (the "Scully Effect": medium/heavy viewers 50% more likely to have worked in STEM, Geena Davis Institute, 2018). This is where social mission and commercial differentiation are jointly stress-tested.

**Section I prices the experience.** It identifies the most-likely package and a reasonable price for a complete STEM story experience, calibrated against proven premium recurring spend in the category (Lovevery's $692.38 lifetime value, Bloomberg Second Measure, 2021) and the broad US enrichment budget already in play.

**Section J is the qualitative goldmine,** capturing unprompted product wishes, disengagement triggers, and parent-designed kits, the open-text layer that turns confirmatory findings into product specification.

### Methodology intent and next-step milestones

The instrument is intentionally mixed-method: closed scales for benchmarkable quantitative comparison against the dossier, paired with open-ended prompts that protect against confirmation bias by letting unmet needs surface unprompted. Each closed item is mapped to an external benchmark, so survey results can be read as convergent or divergent with the national picture rather than in isolation.

The validation roadmap is staged. The near-term milestone is fielding the survey to a sufficient, demographically representative US sample to establish baseline concept appeal (Section F), a demand-ranked kit roadmap (Section G), and an evidenced price band (Section I). Subsequent milestones move from stated to revealed demand: a landing-page or waitlist conversion test, a paid pre-order or pilot cohort to measure real purchase rather than intent, and an early-product engagement and retention study, the metric that most directly answers the churn risk facing single-format subscriptions (more than one-third of US subscribers cancel within three months, McKinsey, 2018). Together these steps move PARI STEAM World from "the secondary data says a gap exists" to "our primary research shows this product fills it."

dossier.dimension: The State of US STEM Education & Declining Student Interest
dossier.summary:
US STEM education is in a documented, deepening crisis at exactly the foundational stage PARI STEAM World targets. The most recent Nation's Report Card (NAEP), released in 2025 for the 2024 assessment, shows American eighth graders at their lowest science performance in over a decade: only 31% reached NAEP Proficient (down 4 points from 2019) and 38% fell below NAEP Basic, the highest share since 2009. Twelfth-grade results hit historic lows, with just 22% proficient in math (45% below NAEP Basic, the largest share ever recorded) and 35% proficient in reading (32% below Basic, also a record). Between 2019 and 2024, NAEP math scores fell 3 points in grade 4 and 8 points in grade 8, with reading down 5 points at each grade. These declines, concentrated among the lowest performers, pre-dated COVID-19 and worsened through it.

Internationally, the United States is a middling-to-lagging performer in foundational STEM subjects. On PISA 2022, US 15-year-olds scored 465 in mathematics, below the OECD average, with 25 education systems scoring higher; science (499) trailed 9 systems and reading (504) trailed 5. Math is the relative weak spot, the very domain where early interest and confidence are formed.

A core structural cause is the marginalization of science in the early grades. The 2018 National Survey of Science and Mathematics Education found K-3 classrooms devote only about 18 minutes a day to science, versus 89 minutes for English language arts and 57 for math, a reflection of decades of curriculum narrowing under standardized-testing pressure. Children are largely not exposed to science during the early-childhood window when interest and identity form. The result is a wide interest-to-intent gap: while 75% of US Gen Z report interest in STEM, only 29% list a STEM role as their first-choice career, and that interest is sharply gender-skewed (63% of girls vs 85% of boys). A pandemic-era gender gap in 8th-grade NAEP science has also re-emerged, with boys outscoring girls by a statistically significant 2 points in 2024 after the gap was not significant in 2019.

Meanwhile, demand is surging. BLS projects STEM occupations will grow 10.4% from 2023 to 2033, nearly triple the 3.6% projected for non-STEM jobs, and STEM roles already pay a median $101,650 versus $46,680 for non-STEM. NCSES counts 36 million STEM workers, about a quarter of the US workforce. The mismatch is stark: rising, well-paid demand for STEM skills colliding with falling achievement, eroding early-grade science instruction, and interest that converts poorly to commitment. That gap is the white space PARI STEAM World addresses, building durable STEM interest and competence in early childhood, before the documented decline sets in.

dossier.dimension: Early Childhood: When STEM Identity Forms
dossier.summary:
The US evidence base points to a striking mismatch: children's attitudes toward science and their self-concept as a "science person" begin forming in early childhood, yet the US education system devotes almost no instructional time to science in exactly those grades. Gender stereotypes that steer children toward or away from "really, really smart" pursuits are measurable by age 6 — and were not present at age 5 — in the landmark study by Bian, Leslie, and Cimpian (Science, 2017). Racial and ethnic gaps in advanced (above-90th-percentile) science and math achievement are already visible at kindergarten entry and remain stable or widen through 5th grade (Morgan et al., Educational Researcher, 2023). And across six US longitudinal datasets, school-entry (kindergarten) math skill is the single strongest predictor of later achievement in both math and reading (Duncan et al., Developmental Psychology, 2007) — meaning the foundation for STEM trajectories is laid before formal science instruction typically begins.

Despite this, US self-contained elementary classrooms spend an average of only about 18 minutes per day on science in grades K-3 and 27 minutes per day in grades 4-6, versus 89 and 82 minutes on reading/language arts and 57 and 63 minutes on mathematics (2018 NSSME+, Horizon Research). Science is taught every day of the week, every week of the year in only 17% of K-3 classes and 35% of grades 4-6 classes. Compounding the time gap, only 31% of self-contained elementary teachers feel "very well prepared" to teach science (vs. 77% for reading and 73% for math), and only about 3% hold a degree in a science field. The result is an early-window opportunity that is structurally underused precisely when identity and interest are most malleable.

The downstream consequences are visible in attitudinal, comparative, and equity data. The share of US 8th-graders reporting a high level of interest and enjoyment in science fell from 38% in 2019 to 28% in 2024 on the NAEP science assessment, with a parallel decline in hands-on scientific inquiry participation. By age 15, US science literacy is middling rather than leading: on PISA 2022 the US averaged 499 versus an OECD average of 485, but 9 of the 80 other participating systems outscored it. By adulthood, women make up only about 26% of the US STEM workforce. Economic research on US early-childhood programs (Heckman et al.) documents returns of about 13% per year, underscoring that early, high-quality exposure is among the highest-ROI interventions available — yet the early grades, where science identity forms, receive the least science.
