dossier.summary:
Despite earning roughly half of all U.S. science and engineering (S&E) bachelor's degrees and making up nearly half of the total workforce, women remain about 35% of the U.S. STEM workforce (2023) and only about 27% of core science and engineering occupations. The gap is starkest in exactly the fields PARI STEAM World touches: engineering and computing. Women hold roughly 16% of U.S. engineering jobs and about 26% of computer and mathematical science jobs, and they earn only about a quarter of engineering and computer-science bachelor's degrees (24% and 22%, respectively, in 2021). The pipeline narrows long before college: women's near-parity in S&E degrees collapses to ~27% of S&E occupations, pointing to attrition rooted in identity and belonging, not aptitude.

A body of landmark U.S. developmental research shows these gaps are seeded in early childhood — the window (roughly ages 3-8) PARI STEAM World targets. Bian, Leslie, and Cimpian's 2017 Science study found that by age 6, girls become less likely than boys to associate being "really, really smart" (brilliance) with their own gender, and begin avoiding activities framed as being for the "really smart." Miller et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis of five decades of U.S. "Draw-A-Scientist" studies (78 studies, 20,000+ children) shows that while children draw female scientists far more than they did in the 1960s (under 1% then vs. 28% in 1985-2016), the association of science with men still strengthens sharply with age: about 70% of 6-year-old girls draw a woman scientist, but only ~25% of 16-year-old girls do. A national survey of U.S. teens likewise found girls' interest in STEM careers fell to 9% versus 27% for boys.

The evidence also points to a clear, intervenable lever — role models — and a clear deficit in supply. Rigorous U.S. studies summarized by J-PAL show that exposure to female role models meaningfully shifts girls' STEM persistence: a single guest talk by a woman economist raised women's likelihood of majoring in economics by 8 percentage points (from 9% to 17%); a female intro-course professor closed about 75% of the gender gap in math/science grades; and same-gender role-model exposure raised high-performing women's choice of underrepresented STEM majors by up to 26 percentage points. Yet children's and family media still underrepresent women as STEM protagonists: across 15 years of top U.S. TV and film, women were only 37-38% of STEM characters (female engineers just 13% and computer scientists 15% in 2018-2022), and 71% of surveyed young people say female STEM representation on-screen is important. This is the white space PARI STEAM World can occupy: girl-forward STEAM characters, role models, and play experiences delivered in the early-childhood window when the brilliance stereotype first takes hold.

dossier.dimension: Market Size: US STEM Toys, Educational Products & EdTech
dossier.summary:
The US market for STEM and educational learning products spans a layered set of segments, all showing above-average growth into 2030, but the verifiable US-specific figures are smaller than some headline numbers suggest. At the hands-on product level, pure-play STEM toys are a small but fast-growing niche: Grand View Research sizes the North America STEM toys market at USD 425.9 million in 2024, rising to ~USD 629.2 million by 2030 at a 6.6% CAGR, of which the US holds a dominant ~80% share — implying a US STEM toys market on the order of USD 340 million in 2024. The broader US educational toys category is far larger, estimated at USD 12.19 billion in 2023 and growing at a 10.8% CAGR (2024-2030), with STEM-specific demand inside that category the fastest-growing sub-segment at a 15.0% CAGR. (Note: GVR publishes two US educational-toys datasets; its Horizon outlook projects the US category to ~USD 13.66 billion by 2030, so the verified, self-consistent endpoint is ~USD 13.66B, not higher figures sometimes quoted.) The signal that holds up: STEM is the growth engine of the educational-toys category but remains under-penetrated relative to total educational-toy spend.

The digital and services layers are an order of magnitude larger and growing faster. The US education technology (EdTech) market generated USD 47.74 billion in 2024 and is forecast to reach USD 90.61 billion by 2030 (11.1% CAGR), with K-12 the largest sector and preschool the fastest-growing — a direct signal that early-childhood digital learning is the highest-momentum slice. The US AI-in-education market is the steepest curve measured, projected to reach USD 8.84 billion by 2030 at a 31.2% CAGR. Supplemental education is also sizable: the US online private tutoring market was USD 4.33 billion in 2024, heading to USD 8.09 billion by 2030 (11.1% CAGR), nested within a total US private tutoring market estimated near USD 39.6 billion (2024, Global Industry Analysts), which Technavio projects to grow by USD 28.85 billion over 2024/2025-2029. Institutional demand is strong too: the US STEM-in-K-12 market was USD 14.12 billion in 2023, projected to USD 46.26 billion by 2032 (~14.1% CAGR, SNS Insider). At the macro level, the US K-12 education market overall was USD 821.6 billion in 2024, projected to USD 1,518.4 billion by 2030 (10.8% CAGR), with the US accounting for 29.4% of the global K-12 market.

All retained figures are US-specific (or, where noted, a clearly labeled global benchmark), sourced primarily from Grand View Research US-segment reports, with corroborating figures from Global Industry Analysts, Technavio, SNS Insider, and Fortune Business Insights. A global/North-America-only kids subscription-box statistic that appeared in the draft was dropped because no clean US-only figure could be verified, and the previously claimed US educational-toys 2030 endpoint of ~USD 24.86B and a STEM-in-K-12 North America share of 44.6% could not be verified and were removed or corrected.

dossier.summary:
US parents place exceptionally high value on STEM and educational development, yet are largely unaware of how far behind their children actually are - a combination that creates strong latent demand for accessible, trustworthy early-STEAM learning products. A Toy Association survey of 2,000 US parents found 76% want their child to end up in a STEM-related career, and STEM occupations in the US are projected to grow far faster than non-STEM jobs (7% vs 2% for 2022-2032 per BLS, with science-and-engineering occupations growing 12.5%, per NSF/NCSES), giving parents a concrete, future-oriented reason to invest early. At the same time, most US adults rate K-12 STEM education as merely average or below: only 28% call it 'best in the world or above average' and 32% call it below average or the worst (Pew 2024), while US 15-year-olds ranked 28th of 37 OECD nations in math on the 2022 PISA - reinforcing parental anxiety that the school system alone will not equip their kids.

A striking 'perception gap' amplifies the opportunity. The Gallup / Learning Heroes 'B-flation' study (2023) found 89% of parents believe their child is at or above grade level in reading and math, while national test data show far fewer students are actually proficient - and worry rises sharply once parents learn the truth (97% of parents who know their child is below grade level in math are worried about it). As awareness tools spread, more parents are likely to seek supplemental learning solutions.

This concern translates into real and growing spending. US enrichment spending is steep and unequal: high-income families spend roughly $8,900 per child per year on enrichment versus about $1,300 for the lowest-income quintile - a gap that widened from ~4x to ~7x over recent decades (Hamilton Project, Duncan & Murnane data). Even mainstream back-to-school outlays are substantial, projected at about $886 per household in 2025 (Empower) after NRF recorded $890.07 per K-12 family in 2023. Parents overwhelmingly prioritize educational value in purchases: a Toy Association survey of US parents found 94% see toys as significant to child development and 91% emphasize the importance of educational toys, while 78% want more toys that build skills like creativity and problem-solving - a clear signal of demand for hands-on, developmental play over passive entertainment.

The market is sizing up accordingly. The US educational toys market was valued at roughly $11.1 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach about $24.6 billion by 2033 (Custom Market Insights, 9.2% CAGR), and hands-on educational subscription kits demonstrate that US parents will pay premium, recurring prices for curated STEAM/developmental experiences - Lovevery's lifetime sales per customer reached $692.38 after 24 months, more than double KiwiCo's and Little Passports' (Bloomberg Second Measure). Meanwhile parents remain ambivalent about screens (roughly 75-80% express concern about screen media per Common Sense Media, even as children age 8 and under average about 2.5 hours of screen time per day), strengthening the appeal of tactile, screen-light STEAM learning.

dossier.dimension: The Screen-Time Crisis & Demand for Hands-On Learning
dossier.summary:
US children are immersed in screens from infancy, and the gap between actual usage and pediatric guidance is wide. The 2025 Common Sense Census (Common Sense Media's flagship national study) finds that screen exposure now begins in the first years of life: children under age 2 average about 1 hour 3 minutes of screen media a day, ages 2-4 average roughly 2 hours 8 minutes, and ages 5-8 average roughly 3 hours 28 minutes. Device ownership has pushed deep into early childhood: 40% of children have their own tablet by age 2 and nearly 1 in 4 have a personal cellphone by age 8. While overall daily screen time for kids 8 and under has held steady at about 2.5 hours, the composition has shifted toward gaming (up 65% in four years) and short-form video. This collides with the American Academy of Pediatrics' guidance, which discourages screen media (other than video chatting) for children younger than 18 months and recommends limiting screen use to 1 hour per day of high-quality programming for ages 2-5, reserving time for free play, sleep, and physical activity.

Concern is mainstream, not fringe. Pew Research Center's October 2025 national survey of parents of children 12 and under shows that 42% feel they could be doing a better job managing their child's screen time, and 80% say social media's harms for kids outweigh its benefits. The federal government has elevated the issue to a public-health level: the 2023 US Surgeon General's Advisory documents that up to 95% of youth 13-17 use a social media platform (more than a third "almost constantly") and nearly 40% of 8-12 year-olds use social media, while citing a US cohort study showing adolescents spending more than 3 hours a day on social media face roughly double the risk of depression and anxiety symptoms. Peer-reviewed US research reinforces the wellbeing link: in a population-based study of the National Survey of Children's Health, 14-17 year-old high screen users (7+ hours/day) were more than twice as likely to have been diagnosed with depression or anxiety than low users (1 hour/day).

The flip side of this anxiety is real, monetizable demand for screen-free, hands-on alternatives. The Toy Association reports that 78% of US parents want more toys that build skills like creativity and problem-solving, and "screen-free play" and maker-style, open-ended kits are flagged as leading trends. Market sizing confirms the commercial pull: the US educational toys market was about USD 12.19 billion in 2023 and is projected to roughly double to about USD 24.86 billion by 2030 at a ~10.8% CAGR, with STEM/hands-on learning cited as a primary growth driver. The US STEM toys segment specifically was about USD 1.8 billion in 2024, accounting for roughly 85% of the North American STEM toys market.

Together these data describe a clear white space: parents are anxious about excessive screen use, pediatric and federal authorities are urging less of it, and there is documented, growing willingness to spend on hands-on, creativity-building, screen-free experiences for young children. A STEAM-focused, offline early-learning concept is positioned directly into the gap between heavy screen reality and the unmet demand for healthy, hands-on alternatives.

dossier.summary:
The US children's STEM learning market is large, fast-growing, and highly fragmented across distinct, non-integrated product models. The US educational toys market was valued at roughly $11.1 billion in 2024 and is projected to more than double to ~$24.6 billion by 2033 (9.2% CAGR), reflecting strong parental appetite for learning-focused products. Yet the offerings competing for this spend are siloed by format: physical-kit subscriptions, one-off STEM kits, and screen-based apps each occupy a separate lane, and almost none combine serialized story, a physical kit, and an AI companion in one product.

Profiling the major US-available players makes the fragmentation concrete. KiwiCo is a physical-kit subscription at $23.95/month for its core crates, rising to $32.95/month for its premium Maker and Eureka crates, and is kit-only with no app or narrative spine. Lovevery's Play Kits are a Montessori toy subscription at an effective ~$40/month (baby kits $80 every 2 months; toddler kits $120 every 3 months), again kit-only. MEL Science is a science-kit subscription at $34.90/month ($25.90/month on an annual plan), pairing kits with companion app/AR content but no serialized characters. Osmo is an app-plus-physical-pieces system sold as a one-time purchase (Genius Starter Kit ~$90 list, frequently discounted), tied to a tablet. Khan Academy Kids is a 100% free app, pure software with no physical component. Each solves one slice — kit, app, or both without story — so a parent who wants hands-on building, screen-based reinforcement, narrative motivation, and adaptive guidance must stitch together several separate products and bills.

This format fragmentation is compounded by a churn problem that punishes single-format subscriptions. McKinsey's US research (a survey of more than 5,000 US consumers) found that more than one-third of subscription consumers cancel within three months and over half within six, with nearly 40% of subscribers ultimately canceling; for curation/access boxes the single most-cited reason for canceling is "not getting value for the money" (29%). Independent industry benchmarks put subscription-box monthly churn commonly at 10-15%. A product that sustains engagement through serialized storytelling and a persistent companion has a structural retention advantage over a box that simply ships another disconnected craft each month.

The clearest white space is the intersection of (a) integrated story + physical kit + AI companion and (b) diverse girl protagonists as role models. US data shows the audience is ready: children 0-8 already average ~2.5 hours of daily screen time and 40% have a tablet by age 2, so a blended physical-plus-digital experience meets kids where they are. At the same time, the role-model gap is acute and quantified — women are only 27% of the US STEM workforce despite being 48% of all workers (2019), teen girls' interest in STEM careers fell to 9% (from 11%) versus 27% for boys, and the share of US girls who believe they are good at math and science dropped from 73% (2017) to 59%. No major incumbent centers diverse girl heroes inside an integrated story-kit-AI format, leaving an unoccupied position that is both commercially differentiated and aligned with a documented social need.

dossier.dimension: Evidence: Storytelling, Representation & AI in STEM Learning
dossier.summary:
US evidence converges on a clear pedagogical case for a story-driven, hands-on, parent-governed-AI STEM model: active doing beats passive transmission, relatable STEM characters change girls' aspirations and real career behavior, and carefully supervised AI produces learning gains while unsupervised AI raises real trust concerns. The strongest causal evidence for "doing over listening" is Freeman et al.'s landmark 2014 PNAS meta-analysis of 225 undergraduate STEM courses: active learning raised exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations (about a half-letter-grade bump) and students in traditional lecture courses were about 1.5x more likely to fail (failure odds ratio 1.95). The study is at the university level, so it is directional rather than dispositive for early childhood, but it is the most-cited evidence that engagement-based instruction beats passive lecturing and it supports project-based and maker approaches earlier in the pipeline.

On representation and storytelling, the Geena Davis Institute / 21st Century Fox "Scully Effect" study (US sample of ~2,000 women aged 25+) found that 63% of women who work in STEM said the fictional scientist Dana Scully was their personal role model, 91% saw her as a role model for girls and women, and 63% of women familiar with Scully said she increased their confidence to excel in a male-dominated profession. Crucially, this character identification tracked with real behavior: medium/heavy female viewers of The X-Files were 50% more likely to have actually worked in a STEM field than non/light viewers (24% vs 16%), and 50% of women familiar with Scully said she increased their interest in STEM. The flip side is a documented confidence crisis the concept can address: ROX's Girls' Index, a national school-based survey of 17,502 US girls in grades 5-12, found the share who believe they are good at math and science fell from 73% (2017) to 59% even as stated STEM interest rose to 55% (from 45%) — a widening interest-versus-confidence gap, with the sharpest early-grade collapse in self-belief.

On AI, US studies show genuine learning gains when AI augments human guidance rather than replacing it. Stanford's Tutor CoPilot randomized controlled trial (900 tutors and ~1,800 K-12 students in a Southern US, majority-Hispanic Title I district) found students of AI-assisted tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to master math topics, rising to 9 points for students of the lowest-rated tutors. But adoption is outpacing trust: the share of US teens using ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled to 26% in 2024, a quarter of US public-school teachers say AI does more harm than good in K-12, and 72% of US teens have used an AI companion (52% regularly) — with about a third finding AI conversations as satisfying as or more satisfying than those with real friends — fueling screen-balance, trust, and child-data concerns.

The market-gap implication is a white space for an early-STEM product that is story-and-character-driven, hands-on, and uses AI as a supervised, parent-trusted layer rather than an unsupervised screen substitute.

keyStats.sourceTitle: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise

keyStats.statistic: 25% of US K-12 public school teachers say AI tools do more harm than good in education; only 6% say more good than harm, 32% say an equal mix, and 35% are unsure.
keyStats.context: Nationally representative survey of 2,531 US public school teachers. Quantifies educator distrust and uncertainty about AI in the classroom — a key adoption barrier the concept must design around.
keyStats.sourceTitle: A quarter of U.S. teachers say AI tools do more harm than good in K-12 education

keyStats.statistic: 72% of US teens have used an AI companion at least once and 52% are regular users; about 1 in 3 (33%) find conversations with AI companions as satisfying as or more satisfying than those with real-life friends.
keyStats.context: Nationally representative survey of 1,060 US teens (ages 13-17), conducted with NORC at the University of Chicago. Shows mainstream AI penetration plus the screen-balance and over-reliance concerns parents have about AI replacing real interaction.
keyStats.sourceTitle: Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions

keyStats.statistic: The share of US teens (13-17) using ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled from 13% (2023) to 26% (2024); among Black and Hispanic teens it was 31% each vs 22% of White teens.
keyStats.context: Nationally representative Pew survey of 1,391 US teens. Confirms rapid, uneven AI adoption among students — demand is real but racing ahead of guidance and parental comfort.
keyStats.sourceTitle: About a quarter of U.S. teens have used ChatGPT for schoolwork — double the share in 2023

keyStats.statistic: Women hold less than a quarter (24%) of US STEM jobs despite making up about half (48%) of the college-educated workforce.
keyStats.context: Cited in the Scully Effect report as the structural gap the concept addresses — establishes the size of the representation shortfall that storytelling and role models aim to narrow at the earliest ages.
keyStats.sourceOrg: Geena Davis Institute on Gender in Media / 21st Century Fox (citing US workforce data)
keyStats.sourceTitle: The 'Scully Effect': I Want to Believe... in STEM

dossier.marketGapImplication: There is clear white space for an early-STEM product that fuses three things US evidence independently validates but that existing offerings rarely combine: (1) narrative/story-driven content with relatable STEM characters — proven to raise girls' STEM confidence, aspirations, and real career behavior (Scully Effect: 63% role-model rate among women in STEM; medium/heavy viewers 50% more likely to have worked in STEM, 24% vs 16%); (2) hands-on, active, project-based doing rather than passive screen consumption — the instructional approach with the strongest causal evidence of learning gains (Freeman: +0.47 SD, failure odds ratio 1.95); and (3) AI used as a supervised, parent- and teacher-trusted assist layer rather than an unsupervised companion. The AI evidence is double-edged: it produces real gains when augmenting human guidance (Tutor CoPilot +4 to +9 pp math mastery) but triggers acute trust and screen-balance concerns (25% of teachers say AI does more harm than good; 72% of teens already use AI companions, 52% regularly; one-third find AI as satisfying as or more satisfying than real friends). Meanwhile the underlying need is urgent and worsening: US girls' STEM confidence has fallen (good-at-math/science 73%->59%; early-grade self-doubt about being smart enough 23%->52%) even as interest rises, and women still hold only 24% of US STEM jobs. The gap is a story-first, hands-on, representation-rich early STEM experience that treats AI as a trustworthy, transparent, parent-governed co-pilot — directly answering both the confidence/representation deficit and the parental distrust that currently caps AI-in-learning adoption.
